title: Paradoxes: Liars, Heaps and Incompleteness
subtitle: When perfectly good reasoning leads somewhere impossible
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain what makes a paradox different from a simple mistake, and state the Liar, the Sorites and Russell's paradox precisely.
By the end you will be able to compare the main responses to the Liar: Tarski's hierarchy, Kripke's truth-value gaps and Priest's dialetheism.
By the end you will be able to evaluate the leading theories of vagueness: epistemicism, supervaluationism and degrees of truth.
By the end you will be able to state Gödel's two incompleteness theorems in plain language and explain how the proof borrows the structure of the Liar.
By the end you will be able to recognize common misuses of Gödel's theorems and explain what they do and do not show.
hook:
Read this sentence carefully: *This sentence is false.* Is it true? If it is true, then what it says holds, so it is false. Is it false? Then what it says is not the case, so it is true. Every exit leads back into the room.

Now a second puzzle. One grain of sand is not a heap. Adding a single grain to something that is not a heap never turns it into a heap. So two grains are not a heap, nor three, nor, after a million patient steps, a million grains. Yet a million grains plainly *is* a heap.

A **paradox** is an argument that starts from premises that seem true, proceeds by steps that seem valid, and arrives at a conclusion that seems false or contradictory. Something has to give, but nothing obviously does. In this final logic lesson we turn the tools of Lessons 1 to 4 on the hardest knots in the subject, and finish with Kurt Gödel's discovery that the Liar's trick, refined, reveals a permanent limit on what any formal system can prove.

sections.heading: What a Paradox Teaches
sections.body:
Not every puzzle is a real paradox. Some only look paradoxical until you spot a hidden error. Zeno's paradoxes of motion (Day 5) are often thought to have been defused, at least mathematically, by the modern theory of limits, which shows that infinitely many shrinking distances can add up to a finite one. Philosophers sometimes call such cases **falsidical**: the argument contains a mistake once you find it.

Others are what W. V. Quine called **antinomies**: they produce a contradiction from principles we seem unable to live without. These force a revision of something deep in our concepts. The three paradoxes in this lesson are of that kind. Each targets a principle that looks like common sense:
- The **Liar** targets our concept of truth, in particular the simple principle that saying a sentence is true is equivalent to asserting the sentence itself.
- The **Sorites** (from the Greek *soros*, heap) targets classical logic's assumption that every statement is either true or false, applied to vague words.
- **Russell's paradox** targets the natural idea that any condition you can state defines a collection.

A useful method: list a paradox's ingredients and ask which you are prepared to give up. Every solution pays some price.

Remarkably, two of these puzzles are attributed to the same man, Eubulides of Miletus, a philosopher of the Megarian school in the 4th century BCE and a rival of Aristotle. That neither has an agreed solution after some 2,400 years tells you something about their depth.

sections.heading: The Liar and the Theory of Truth
sections.body:
A popular ancestor of the Liar is Epimenides the Cretan, who is reported to have said that Cretans are always liars. Strictly, that version is not paradoxical: the statement can simply be false, provided some Cretan, sometime, told the truth. The sharp version is self-referential: "This sentence is false," or the **strengthened Liar**, "This sentence is not true."

The ingredients are few:
1. Self-reference: we can form a sentence L that says of itself that it is not true.
2. The **T-schema**: for any sentence S, "S" is true if and only if S. ("Snow is white" is true if and only if snow is white.)
3. Classical logic, including the law of excluded middle (every sentence is true or not true) and the rule that a contradiction is unacceptable.

Apply the T-schema to L: L is true if and only if L is not true. Under classical logic, that is a contradiction. So which ingredient goes?

**Tarski's hierarchy.** In a celebrated 1933 paper, the Polish logician Alfred Tarski showed how to define truth rigorously for formal languages, building in the T-schema. But he also proved that a sufficiently rich language cannot contain its own truth predicate without contradiction. His solution was to stratify: the predicate "true" for an **object language** belongs to a separate **metalanguage**, whose own truth predicate belongs to a meta-metalanguage, and so on. No sentence can say of itself that it is true, so L cannot be formed. This works beautifully for mathematics, but it fits natural language poorly. In English, "true" applies to English sentences, and we cannot always tell which level we are speaking at.

**Kripke's gaps.** In "Outline of a Theory of Truth" (1975), Saul Kripke offered a single language containing its own truth predicate. Imagine building up truth in stages: first we declare true the ordinary sentences about the world ("Snow is white"), then sentences that say those are true, and so on, until the process reaches a stable point, a **fixed point**. Sentences that never get settled, like L, are **ungrounded**: they fall into a **truth-value gap**, neither true nor false. The cost is the **revenge problem**. Consider: "This sentence is either false or gappy." If it is gappy, it is true; if it is true, it is false or gappy. The paradox returns one level up, and Kripke himself acknowledged that his own description of the gaps had to be given in a richer metalanguage.

**Dialetheism.** Graham Priest, beginning in the late 1970s and in *In Contradiction* (1987), takes the boldest line: the Liar is both true and false. A **dialetheia** is a true contradiction. To make this livable, Priest abandons the classical rule of **explosion** (*ex falso quodlibet*: from a contradiction, anything follows), which you met implicitly in Lesson 1's truth tables, where a false antecedent makes any conditional true. In a **paraconsistent logic**, a contradiction in one corner does not spread to everything. Most logicians reject dialetheism, but Priest has made the law of non-contradiction, which Aristotle (Day 17) called the firmest of all principles, a live topic of debate.

sections.heading: Heaps, Baldness and the Problem of Vagueness
sections.body:
The Sorites does not need self-reference at all. It needs only a **vague** predicate: one with **borderline cases** and no sharp boundary. "Heap," "bald," "tall," "child," "red" and "rich" are all vague. Formally the argument is a chain of modus ponens steps (Lesson 1):
1. A man with 0 hairs is bald.
2. For every n, if a man with n hairs is bald, then a man with n + 1 hairs is bald.
3. Therefore, a man with 150,000 hairs is bald.

Premise 1 is true, the conclusion is false, and each step is valid. So premise 2, the **tolerance principle**, looks like the culprit. But denying it seems to commit us to a sharp cutoff: some number n such that n hairs is bald and n + 1 is not. Can that be right? Three main theories respond.

**Epistemicism.** Timothy Williamson (*Vagueness*, 1994) and Roy Sorensen bite the bullet: there really is a sharp cutoff, we just cannot know where it is. Classical logic is kept intact. Vagueness is a kind of ignorance, rooted in the fact that the meaning of "bald" is fixed by the whole messy pattern of how speakers use it, and our knowledge needs a margin for error. The cost is credibility: many find it incredible that one hair could make the difference between bald and not bald, even an unknowable one.

**Supervaluationism.** Kit Fine (1975) suggested that a vague word can be made precise in many acceptable ways, called **sharpenings**. "Bald" might be sharpened to "fewer than 1,000 hairs" or "fewer than 1,200". A statement is **supertrue** if it is true on every acceptable sharpening, superfalse if false on all, and indeterminate otherwise. "A man with 1,100 hairs is bald" is indeterminate. Beautifully, "There is a cutoff somewhere" comes out supertrue, since every sharpening has one, yet there is no particular number n of which it is supertrue that n is the cutoff. The costs: some classical patterns of reasoning fail, and a statement like "Either he is bald or he is not" is supertrue even though neither disjunct is.

**Degrees of truth.** Inspired by Lotfi Zadeh's **fuzzy logic** (1965), this view assigns truth values between 0 and 1. "A man with 1,100 hairs is bald" might be true to degree 0.6. Each step of the Sorites loses a tiny amount of truth, so the conclusion can be wholly false while each conditional is nearly true. The cost: the boundary problem reappears. Is there a sharp line between "true to degree 1" and "true to degree less than 1"? This is the problem of **higher-order vagueness**: the borderline cases seem to have borderline cases of their own, and every theory must say something about it.

sections.heading: Russell's Paradox Revisited
sections.body:
On Day 69 you met the episode that shook the foundations of mathematics. Gottlob Frege had tried to derive arithmetic from pure logic, using a principle (his Basic Law V) that amounted to this: for any condition, there is a set of exactly the things meeting that condition. This **naive comprehension** principle looks harmless. There is a set of red things, a set of prime numbers, even a set of sets.

In 1901 Bertrand Russell considered the condition "is not a member of itself." Most sets are not members of themselves (the set of cats is not a cat). Let R be the set of all sets that are not members of themselves. Is R a member of R?
- If R is in R, then it meets R's condition, so it is not a member of itself.
- If R is not in R, it meets the condition, so it is in R.

In symbols, using Lesson 2's notation: R ∈ R ↔ ¬(R ∈ R). That is a contradiction derived from comprehension and logic alone. Russell wrote to Frege in June 1902, as the second volume of Frege's *Basic Laws of Arithmetic* was in press. Frege added an appendix acknowledging that the foundations of his work had been shaken.

The popular **barber** version (a barber shaves all and only those who do not shave themselves; who shaves the barber?) is not a genuine paradox: it simply proves no such barber exists. Russell's paradox is deeper because naive comprehension seemed to be a law of logic.

Notice the family resemblance with the Liar. Both involve **self-reference** and **negation**, and both use a technique called **diagonalization**, which Georg Cantor had used in the 1890s to prove that there are more real numbers than natural numbers: you build an object that differs from every item in a list by disagreeing with each item about itself.

Two responses became standard. Russell's own **theory of types**, developed in *Principia Mathematica* (with A. N. Whitehead, 1910–13), sorts objects into levels: individuals, sets of individuals, sets of sets, and so on. A set can contain only things of a lower type, so "x ∈ x" is not even grammatical, just as Tarski would later forbid a sentence from calling itself true. The other, **Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory** (ZF), the working foundation of most mathematics today, drops naive comprehension and replaces it with more cautious axioms: you can only carve a subset out of a set you already have. R never gets built.

sections.heading: Gödel: Turning the Liar into a Theorem
sections.body:
By the 1920s the mathematician David Hilbert had set out a program: formalize all of mathematics in a system of axioms, then prove, by secure finite methods, that the system is **consistent** (never proves a contradiction) and **complete** (proves every true statement in its language, or rather, for every statement, proves it or its negation). In 1930, at a conference in Königsberg, a 24-year-old Austrian logician named Kurt Gödel quietly announced a result that showed this program could not be carried out. The paper appeared in 1931.

Gödel's key idea was to make arithmetic talk about itself. Using **Gödel numbering**, every symbol, formula and proof is coded as a natural number, so statements about formulas and proofs become statements about numbers. "This sequence of formulas is a proof of that formula" becomes an arithmetical relation between two numbers, which the system itself can express.

Then comes the Liar, with one crucial change. Instead of "This sentence is not true," Gödel constructed (by a diagonal technique) a sentence G that in effect says: **"G is not provable in this system."** Now reason:
- If G were provable, the system would prove something false (since G says it is not provable), so a consistent system cannot prove it.
- So, if the system is consistent, G is not provable. But that is exactly what G says. So G is true.

There is no contradiction here, because "true" and "provable" are different. That gap is the whole discovery.

In plain language, the **First Incompleteness Theorem** says: any consistent formal system, whose axioms can be listed mechanically and which is strong enough to express basic arithmetic, contains statements that it can neither prove nor disprove. (Gödel's original proof assumed a slightly stronger condition than consistency; J. Barkley Rosser removed it in 1936.) Adding G as a new axiom does not help: the new system has its own Gödel sentence.

The **Second Incompleteness Theorem** says that such a system, if consistent, cannot prove its own consistency. Hilbert's hope of a self-certifying foundation was gone.

Five years later Alan Turing (Day 89) proved a cousin result for computation: no program can decide, for every program and input, whether that program will eventually halt. The diagonal argument again: imagine a program that does the opposite of whatever the supposed halting-checker predicts about it.

Few theorems have been so widely misused. Gödel did *not* show that mathematics is inconsistent, that truth is relative, or that "everything is uncertain." The theorems concern formal systems with precise properties. Arguments by J. R. Lucas (1961) and Roger Penrose (*The Emperor's New Mind*, 1989) that Gödel proves the human mind is no machine are contested by most logicians, chiefly because they assume we can know our own reasoning is consistent, which is exactly what the Second Theorem says no such system can establish from within.

keyQuote.text: We must know. We will know.
keyQuote.source: David Hilbert, radio address in Königsberg, 8 September 1930, the day after Gödel first announced his incompleteness result at the same conference

modernConnection.title: Bright Lines, Bug Checkers and the Limits of Machines
modernConnection.body:
Every legal system is a running experiment in the Sorites. Childhood fades into adulthood gradually, yet the law needs an answer to "Can this person vote?" So it draws a **bright line**: 18 years, a blood-alcohol limit of 0.08 percent, a speed limit of 70. These lines are the supervaluationist's sharpenings made official. Lawmakers know the line is arbitrary in the sense that 17 years and 364 days is not morally different from 18, but they accept that cost for predictability. Where the law instead uses vague standards ("reasonable care," "excessive force"), courts must handle borderline cases one at a time. The same choice faces anyone writing rules for an online platform: a precise rule ("no images showing more than X") is easy to apply and easy to game, while a vague standard ("no harassment") tracks what we care about but invites inconsistency. The philosophy of vagueness does not tell you which to choose, but it tells you that you cannot have both perfect precision and perfect fit.

Gödel and Turing, meanwhile, set permanent limits on software. Because of the halting problem, and a generalization proved by Henry Rice in the early 1950s, known as Rice's theorem, no program can perfectly decide any interesting property of the behavior of arbitrary programs: whether they will crash, leak data or contain malware. That is why antivirus software and code analyzers must either miss some problems or raise false alarms, and why engineers verify specific systems with carefully restricted methods, like the model checkers mentioned in Lesson 4, rather than all programs at once.

It is tempting to conclude that these theorems also show artificial intelligence can never match human thought. Be careful: humans are not known to escape these limits either. We cannot decide every halting question, and we have no proof that our own reasoning is consistent. What the theorems do show is more modest and more certain: no system, of silicon or of neurons, will ever be a complete and self-certifying oracle.

vocabulary.definition: An argument from apparently true premises, by apparently valid steps, to an apparently false or contradictory conclusion.
vocabulary.example: The Sorites is a paradox because each premise seems true, yet the conclusion that a million grains is not a heap is absurd.

vocabulary.definition: Tarski's principle that, for any sentence S, the claim that S is true is equivalent to S itself.
vocabulary.example: By the T-schema, "Paris is in France" is true if and only if Paris is in France.

vocabulary.definition: The status of a sentence that is neither true nor false, as Kripke proposed for ungrounded sentences like the Liar.
vocabulary.example: On Kripke's theory, "This sentence is false" falls into a truth-value gap.

vocabulary.definition: The view, defended by Graham Priest, that some contradictions are true, combined with a paraconsistent logic that blocks explosion.
vocabulary.example: A dialetheist says the Liar sentence is both true and false, without concluding that everything follows.

vocabulary.definition: The property of a word that has borderline cases and no apparent sharp boundary of application.
vocabulary.example: "Tall" is vague: someone 5 foot 11 is neither clearly tall nor clearly not.

vocabulary.definition: The theory that a vague statement is true if it comes out true on every acceptable way of making its words precise.
vocabulary.example: For a supervaluationist, "Someone with 2 hairs is bald" is supertrue, while the bald status of a borderline case is indeterminate.

vocabulary.definition: A technique for constructing an object that differs from every item on a list by disagreeing with each item about itself.
vocabulary.example: Cantor, Russell, Gödel and Turing all used diagonalization to build their self-referential results.

vocabulary.definition: The property of a formal system that there are statements in its language it can neither prove nor disprove.
vocabulary.example: Gödel showed that every consistent, effectively axiomatized system strong enough for arithmetic suffers from incompleteness.

thinkingExercise.title: Choose Your Price
thinkingExercise.prompt: Every solution to a paradox gives up something attractive. Work out which price you would pay.
steps: Write out the Sorites for a vague word you use at work or at home ("late," "expensive," "a few"). Make the tolerance premise explicit.
For your example, describe what an epistemicist, a supervaluationist and a degree theorist would each say about the borderline cases.

List the three ingredients of the Liar (self-reference, the T-schema, classical logic). Decide which one you would sacrifice, and write two sentences defending your choice against the strongest objection.
Explain to an imaginary friend, in under 100 words and without symbols, why Gödel's sentence G produces incompleteness rather than a contradiction.
Find a claim in the media or online that invokes Gödel or 'incompleteness' outside mathematics. Judge whether it uses the theorem accurately.

summary: A genuine paradox derives a contradiction from principles we find hard to give up; every solution is a choice about which principle to sacrifice.
The Liar exploits self-reference, the T-schema and classical logic; Tarski stratifies languages, Kripke allows truth-value gaps, and Priest accepts true contradictions with a paraconsistent logic.

The Sorites exploits vague predicates; epistemicism posits unknowable sharp cutoffs, supervaluationism quantifies over precise sharpenings, and degree theories make truth come in amounts, but all face higher-order vagueness.
Russell's paradox refuted naive comprehension and led to type theory and Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory; it shares the self-reference and diagonal structure of the Liar.

Gödel replaced 'true' with 'provable' in the Liar to show that consistent formal systems strong enough for arithmetic are incomplete and cannot prove their own consistency; the theorems are precise and often misused.

quiz.question: Why is Epimenides' claim that 'Cretans are always liars' not a strict paradox?
options: Because Epimenides was not really a Cretan
Because the claim can simply be false if some Cretan once told the truth
Because it is not self-referential at all
Because it is about the future
quiz.explanation: If some Cretan sometime told the truth, the claim is just false and no contradiction follows. The strict Liar ('This sentence is not true') leaves no such exit.

quiz.question: What is the 'revenge problem' for Kripke's theory of truth?
options: Gödel showed the theory was inconsistent
A new sentence, such as 'This sentence is false or gappy', recreates the paradox
It makes all mathematical statements gappy
quiz.explanation: Once gaps are introduced, a sentence that says of itself that it is false or gappy produces a contradiction again, one level up.

quiz.question: Graham Priest's dialetheism holds that the Liar is both true and false, and uses a logic in which a contradiction does not imply everything.
quiz.explanation: Priest rejects explosion (ex falso quodlibet) and adopts a paraconsistent logic so that true contradictions remain contained.

quiz.question: Which theory says that there is a sharp boundary between bald and not bald, but that we cannot know where it is?
quiz.explanation: Epistemicists such as Timothy Williamson keep classical logic and treat vagueness as a form of ignorance.

quiz.question: A city sets the legal drinking age at exactly 21, although no one thinks a person changes overnight. In supervaluationist terms, this is best described as:
options: Choosing one acceptable sharpening of a vague concept
quiz.explanation: The law picks one precise version of the vague notion 'mature enough to drink', just as a sharpening makes a vague word precise.

quiz.question: The barber paradox is just as deep as Russell's paradox, because it shows that logic itself is inconsistent.
quiz.explanation: The barber argument simply proves that no such barber exists. Russell's paradox is deeper because naive comprehension seemed to be a law of logic.

quiz.question: What did Russell's paradox refute?
options: The principle that any stated condition defines a set
quiz.explanation: The set of all sets that are not members of themselves cannot exist, so naive comprehension (Frege's Basic Law V) must be abandoned.

quiz.question: Gödel's sentence G says, in effect, 'G is not provable in this system'. Why does this produce incompleteness rather than a contradiction?
options: Because provability and truth come apart, so G can be true but unprovable
Because G is both true and false
quiz.explanation: Unlike the Liar, G talks about provability. If the system is consistent, G is unprovable, and so what it says is true.

quiz.question: The Second Incompleteness Theorem says that a consistent formal system strong enough for arithmetic cannot prove its own consistency.
quiz.explanation: This defeated Hilbert's hope of a mathematical system that could certify its own reliability from within.

quiz.question: Gödel's theorems show that mathematical truth is relative to culture.
quiz.explanation: The theorems are precise results about formal systems. They say nothing about cultural relativity; indeed G is shown to be true, not relative.

goDeeper.body:
Incompleteness is not only about artificial sentences like G. In 1940 Gödel showed that Georg Cantor's **continuum hypothesis** (that there is no set size strictly between the natural numbers and the real numbers) cannot be disproved from the standard ZF axioms with the axiom of choice (ZFC), assuming those axioms are consistent. In 1963 Paul Cohen showed it cannot be proved either. So a natural question that Hilbert had placed first on his famous 1900 list of problems is independent of the axioms nearly all mathematicians use.

This raises a philosophical question with no settled answer. A **platonist** (recall Plato's Forms on Day 11) holds that sets exist independently of us, so the continuum hypothesis is either true or false, and we simply need better axioms to discover which. Gödel himself held this view and hoped new axioms would settle the question. A **pluralist**, such as Joel David Hamkins, argues instead that there is a "multiverse" of set-theoretic universes, in some of which the hypothesis holds and in others not, with no fact about which is the real one. Here the logic of incompleteness meets the metaphysics of Lesson 4: are mathematical alternatives like possible worlds, all equally legitimate, or is one of them actual?

There are also more down-to-earth independent statements. In 1977 Jeff Paris and Leo Harrington found a natural-looking combinatorial statement, a strengthening of Ramsey's theorem, that is true but unprovable in standard Peano arithmetic. Results like this suggest that incompleteness is not a curiosity at the edges of mathematics but a feature of its landscape.

questions: If you had to give up one ingredient of the Liar, would it be self-reference, the T-schema or classical logic? What would your choice cost elsewhere?
Is there a fact about exactly when a child becomes an adult, even if no one can know it?
Does the existence of true but unprovable statements show that mathematical truth goes beyond any human method of knowing it?
